drills.q: Name the four layers of ML monitoring in order and what each catches.
drills.a: Infra (system falling over) → Data (input no longer matching training assumptions) → Model (model behaving differently before labels exist) → Business (the metric that actually pays, slowest to move).

drills.q: A classifier's accuracy dashboard has been flat for two weeks. Does that mean the model is healthy?
drills.a: Not necessarily — if labels lag two weeks, the accuracy dashboard hasn't seen any post-incident data yet. Check layer-3 (prediction distribution, confidence) for a real-time read instead.

drills.q: Why is average latency a worse metric to alert on than p99 latency?
drills.a: Average hides the tail; a small fraction of very slow requests (which is usually what causes user complaints and cascading failures) can be invisible in an average while dominating p99.

drills.q: Design an alert for prediction-mean drift that won't page on routine weekly seasonality. What's the key change from a static threshold?
drills.a: Compare against a seasonality-aware baseline (same hour/day-of-week last week) and alert on rate-of-change rather than an absolute value; require correlation with a second signal (e.g. a data-layer anomaly) before paging.

drills.q: Walk through the silently-truncated-feature failure mode end to end: what breaks, what stays green, and what catches it.
drills.a: An upstream pipeline truncates a feature; prediction mean steps at the deploy time; null rate stays 0% because the field is populated, just shorter; infra metrics stay flat; accuracy stays flat because labels lag. Only prediction-distribution (layer 3) monitoring, correlated with deploy timestamps, catches it before the label-lag window closes.

drills.q: Your LLM system's monthly cost triples with flat request volume. What do you check first and why?
drills.a: Token counts per request per prompt-template version first — a context-length regression is invisible in latency and error rate but shows up immediately in token counts, and is a far more common cause than a pricing change.

drills.q: Design the logging/sampling strategy for a consumer LLM product doing 5M requests/day, being mindful of both cost and PII exposure.
drills.a: Log 100% of structured metadata (ids, latency, token counts, confidence, model/prompt version) cheaply. Sample 1-10% of full prompt/completion text, oversampling errors and low-confidence/flagged outputs. Redact PII before storage or restrict raw text to a separate, tightly access-controlled store with a short retention window.

drills.q: A fraud model's labels (chargebacks) take 60-90 days. Design real-time monitoring that doesn't rely on those labels.
drills.a: Layer 3 (prediction score distribution, confidence, feature-importance shift) carries the real-time burden. Add a faster proxy label (manual review disagreement, customer-reported disputes) to get a partial ground-truth stream well before the 60-90 day window closes.

drills.q: A model's refusal rate jumps 15% overnight with no deploy on your team's side. Diagnose and prevent recurrence.
drills.a: Check whether the model is pointed at a rolling alias on a managed provider — the provider likely updated safety tuning. Prevent recurrence by pinning an explicit model version and treating refusal rate as a first-class monitored metric with its own alert.

drills.q: How would you measure whether your team's monitoring dashboards are actually being used, and what would you do with a dashboard that scores zero?
drills.a: Track dashboard view events correlated with incident timestamps and general usage over time. A dashboard with zero views outside the week it was built is a signal to delete it or fold its key panel into an existing, actually-used dashboard rather than adding more panels to something nobody opens.

drills.q: Your team wants judge-score monitoring added to all 40 of your production prompt templates. As the reviewing engineer, do you approve it as-is?
drills.a: No — prioritize by request volume and business criticality per template first. Judge calls have real per-call cost; uniformly instrumenting a low-traffic internal tool at the same rigor as a customer-facing flow is misallocated spend.
